MUCUR GRMHD 2D Meridional Plane

An axisymmetric general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics code for accretion flows and jets around rotating (Kerr) black holes. It evolves the full meridional plane (r, θ), from pole to pole, with all three components of velocity and magnetic field.

  • Release v4r
  • Fortran 90 · MPI · PARAMESH
  • Kerr space-time, Boyer–Lindquist and Kerr–Schild
  • 70 modified-gravity and alternative space-times
  • Validated: Blandford–Znajek power, Michel and Bondi inflow, BHL, Wald, magnetised torus

What the code does

The code solves the equations of ideal GRMHD for a perfect fluid with an ideal-gas equation of state on a fixed, stationary, axisymmetric black-hole background. All quantities depend on (t, r, θ), with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. Every velocity, momentum and magnetic-field component is evolved, so the gas can rotate and poloidal field can be wound into a toroidal component. Frame dragging creates toroidal field from poloidal field in exactly this way, so the Blandford–Znajek process works self-consistently in the code.

Integrated rates are totals through a sphere, so the results compare directly with 3D simulations and with analytic accretion formulae.

The release comes with five ready-to-run set-ups and five test problems with exact or published solutions to compare with.

Typical applications

  • Bondi–Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion of a wind moving along the spin axis onto a Kerr black hole, with or without magnetic field
  • Spherical (Bondi, Michel) accretion, with or without a radial field
  • Feeding a spinning hole through an equatorial window with both poles open
  • Magnetised black holes (split monopole), extraction of rotational energy by the Blandford–Znajek process, and jet formation
  • Any axisymmetric initial state: tori, shells, clouds, custom magnetic fields

What you can solve with this code

The code evolves the meridional plane (r, θ) of a black hole from pole to pole, so it is made for problems in which the spin axis matters: jets, polar outflows, flows along the axis and magnetised black holes. Some of the problems it can solve:

Accretion onto black holes

  • Bondi–Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion of a wind moving along the spin axis, with or without magnetic field
  • Spherical (Bondi, Michel) accretion onto rotating and non-rotating holes
  • Gas fed through an equatorial window with both poles open
  • Magnetised low-angular-momentum flows and the oscillations of their shocks
  • Build-up of magnetic flux on the hole and the magnetically arrested state
  • … and many more

Jets and magnetospheres

  • Blandford–Znajek jets: power against spin, magnetic flux, accretion rate and the supply of gas
  • Jets of black holes moving through a magnetised wind or the interstellar medium
  • The jet shape from the horizon to the Bondi radius: parabolic to conical collimation
  • Magnetised black holes: split monopole and Wald field, energy extraction and current sheets
  • Tori with field loops: jet intermittency and flares; collapsar-like infall and jet break-out
  • … and many more

Gravity beyond Kerr

  • Every problem on this page in 70 alternative black-hole space-times
  • How the theory of gravity changes accretion rates, shocks and jet power compared with Kerr
  • The equilibrium spin of black holes that accrete without a disc
  • Models to compare with observed X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei
  • … and many more

Your problem is not on the list? Any initial state, magnetic field and supply of gas can be set up in the user header file. Tell us about it →

Physics and numerical method

ComponentImplementation
EquationsIdeal GRMHD in the Valencia 3+1 conservative formulation. Conserved variables D, Sj, τ, B̃k; geometric sources from the Christoffel symbols; the Sφ source is exactly zero, so angular momentum changes only through boundary fluxes.
Space-timeKerr black hole in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates, or in horizon-penetrating ingoing Kerr–Schild coordinates with the inner boundary inside the horizon. The full θ dependence of the metric is evaluated at cell centres and on both kinds of faces. Any spin, prograde or retrograde. In addition, 70 alternative black-hole space-times from modified gravity and other theories, with the full θ dependence, in Boyer–Lindquist-type coordinates.
Equation of stateIdeal gas, p = (Γ − 1)ρε, with adjustable adiabatic index Γ
Reconstruction and fluxesMinmod reconstruction of ρ, p, vi, Bi; HLLE Riemann solver with the fast-magnetosonic characteristic speeds
Divergence of BFlux-constrained transport keeps ∇·B = 0 to round-off (relative ~10−14), including the cells on the polar axis
Time integrationSecond-order Runge–Kutta with Strang-type splitting of the source terms; Courant time step
Primitive recoveryOne-dimensional Newton–Raphson iteration safeguarded by bisection (Noble et al. type), with an entropy-based fallback where the energy equation has no physical root (highly magnetised cells)
RobustnessDensity and magnetisation floors that add mass at rest in the normal-observer frame; a pressure floor, with a temperature floor set automatically from the injected gas, and an entropy floor; Lorentz-factor and temperature ceilings; optional magnetised atmosphere; optional limits for the cells inside the horizon (Kerr–Schild); a safety stop and full bookkeeping of what the floors add; a start-up check that the Kerr–Schild inner boundary lies outside the inner horizon
Initial statesGrid filled with the injected wind, a Fishbone–Moncrief torus, or your own state; magnetic field none, uniform vertical, split monopole, Wald field, or a torus field loop, with an optional toroidal part
BoundariesReflection at the polar axis θ = 0 and π (zero flux, zero EMF); outflow inner boundary; outer boundary with injection of a BHL wind, spherical inflow, or an equatorial feeding window, with zero-gradient outflow elsewhere; optional absorbing layer near rmax that removes outgoing waves without reflection
Grid and parallelismPARAMESH blocks of 32 × 32 cells, uniform resolution, MPI parallel. Nθ = 256 and Nr = 256 × n (e.g. 512 × 256 up to 2048 × 256)
Run controlCheckpoint and restart, including a wall-clock limit for queue systems; all problem parameters in a single user header file

Beyond Kerr: 70 modified-gravity and alternative space-times

The code is not limited to the Kerr metric. Besides Kerr, it evolves the flow in 70 further black-hole space-times from modified theories of gravity, quantum-corrected and regular black holes, nonlinear electrodynamics, and black holes surrounded by dark matter. With the same code, the same set-up and the same diagnostics, you can see directly how the theory of gravity changes accretion, outflows and jets.

How the metrics are implemented

  • Every space-time has the full θ dependence of the metric, so the whole (r, θ) plane is evolved consistently, not just the equator.
  • The metric derivatives come from the complex-step method, which is exact to round-off.
  • Each metric was checked against the formulas in the literature, its derivatives against finite differences, its north–south symmetry, and its Kerr or Schwarzschild limit.

Good to know

  • The alternative space-times use Boyer–Lindquist-type coordinates, so the grid lies outside the horizon. The code checks this at start-up.
  • The parameters of each theory (couplings, charges, hair, dark-matter density and so on) are set in the user header file.
  • A new space-time can be added from a template and is checked the same way. If the metric you need is not in the list, we can add it.

The computational domain

All set-ups share one grid: the full meridional half-plane rmin ≤ r ≤ rmax, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, with uniform cells in r and θ. Both halves of the spin axis are reflection boundaries, so outflows along the axis in both directions are part of the solution.

In Boyer–Lindquist coordinates the inner boundary lies outside the horizon. In Kerr–Schild coordinates it lies inside the horizon, so the ergosphere and the horizon are both on the grid, the natural choice for jet launching. The code checks at start-up that this boundary stays outside the inner horizon.

At rmax gas is injected where the set-up feeds it: on the upstream hemisphere for a wind along the axis, at all angles for spherical inflow, or through a window around the equator. Elsewhere the boundary lets gas leave freely, and an absorbing layer inside rmax removes outgoing waves without reflection.

Ready-to-run set-ups

The code comes with five complete set-ups, plus the headers of every test problem. Each set-up is one user header file with all its initial and boundary values. To start a new problem, pick the closest set-up and change what you need.

Set-upCoordinates and gridMagnetic field at t = 0Purpose
GRHDBoyer–Lindquist, 2.3 ≤ r ≤ 100 M, 512 × 256NoneHydrodynamic Bondi–Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion along the spin axis; reference for the magnetised runs
GRMHD (default)Boyer–Lindquist, 2.3 ≤ r ≤ 100 M, 512 × 256Uniform vertical field, β0 = 10, also carried by the windMagnetised BHL accretion; flux accumulating on the hole
GRMHD_BHfieldBoyer–Lindquist, 2.3 ≤ r ≤ 100 M, 512 × 256Split monopole on the hole (β = 1 at rmin); unmagnetised windMagnetised black hole in an unmagnetised wind
GRMHD_jet_KSKerr–Schild, 1.0 ≤ r ≤ 100 M, 1024 × 256Uniform vertical field, β0 = 10Jet launching by the Blandford–Znajek process, with the ergosphere and the horizon on the grid
GRMHD_jet_equatorialKerr–Schild, 1.0 ≤ r ≤ 100 M, 1024 × 256Uniform vertical field, β0 = 10; gas injected only in 3π/8 ≤ θ ≤ 5π/8Jets along both open poles, fed by gas that drags magnetic flux onto the hole

The first four inject the same wind along the spin axis onto a Kerr hole with a = 0.9: v∞ = 0.2, cs,∞ = 0.1, ρ∞ = 1, Γ = 4/3 (Mach 2, accretion radius 40 M).

Beyond these, the code can start from a Fishbone–Moncrief torus with a poloidal field loop, a split monopole, the Wald field of a Kerr hole in a uniform field, or any axisymmetric state you write yourself: tori, shells, clouds, custom fields and perturbations.

Blandford–Znajek power of a split monopole (V1–V3)Passed

The standard test for jet physics around a spinning black hole is a split-monopole magnetic field on the hole, in a strongly magnetised plasma (σ = b²/ρ = 50). Frame dragging forces the field lines to rotate, and they carry an outgoing Poynting flux that must match the Blandford–Znajek formula:

PBZ = κ Φ² ΩH²,   κ = (1 + 1.38 ΩH² − 9.2 ΩH⁴) / 6π,   ΩH = a / 2r+

We ran the test for three spins in Kerr–Schild coordinates, with the horizon and the ergosphere on the grid: V1 (a = 0.9) and V2 (a = 0.5) on 1024 × 256 cells, and V3 (a = 0.99) on 2048 × 256 cells with rmax = 100 M, to t = 80 M.

Power ratio measured just outside the horizon (r ≈ 1.1 r+) at t = 50 M; field-line rotation is the median over θ = 10°–80° at r = 3 M. Behind the outgoing front the power ratio is flat in radius to within a few per cent; V3 stays at 0.99 near the horizon at t = 70 M and reproduces an earlier run with rmax = 50 M. At a = 0.99 the measured power agrees with the formula above, including its high-spin correction, to within 1 %; the simple second-order formula ΩH²/6π overestimates it by 8 %.

Spherical accretion: Michel and Bondi flow (V4a, V4b, V5, V6)Passed

Spherical accretion of an ideal gas (Γ = 4/3) onto a non-rotating black hole has an exact solution: the flow is subsonic far out, passes the sonic point (here at 8 M) and falls supersonically through the horizon. The exact state is injected at rmax = 100 M at all angles, and the code must relax to the solution, with the accretion rate Ṁ = 876.13 and the Bernoulli constant −hut = 1.17180 the same at every radius. All five runs of this family have passed, in Kerr–Schild coordinates with the horizon on the grid, to t = 3000 M. None of them used a floor or had a failed inversion or NaN.

Bondi–Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion along the spin axis (B1–B3)Passed

B2: Γ = 5/3 past a Schwarzschild hole

A uniform supersonic wind (Γ = 5/3, v∞ = 0.5, Mach 5) flows along the axis past a Schwarzschild hole, on 1024 × 256 cells to r = 100 M and t = 2000 M. A strong shock forms behind the hole within 150 M and the cone widens until t ≈ 700 M; then the flow is exactly steady and axisymmetric, without the cone oscillations that appear in planar or 3D computations. There is no NaN, no failed inversion and no floor outside the horizon.

  • Ṁ is the same through the four spheres from the accretion radius to 30 M and constant in time to 10−6 after t = 1600 M.
  • Ė/Ṁ equals the Bernoulli constant of the injected wind to 10−5: energy is conserved through the shock.
  • The shock is strong, with a density jump close to the limit of 4, and forms a detached cone whose angle decreases outwards towards the Mach angle.
  • The accretion rate agrees with Font & Ibáñez (1998) to 7 % and the stagnation point to 2.7 M, on a much larger grid than theirs.

B1: softer gas (Γ = 4/3) and the dependence on Γ

B1 uses the same Mach 5 wind past a Schwarzschild hole with Γ = 4/3, on 1024 × 256 cells to t = 2000 M (445 241 steps). The flow becomes steady, Ṁ is the same through the four flux spheres and Ė/Ṁ equals the Bernoulli constant of the wind to 2 × 10−4.

  • A detached shock cone forms, with an opening angle of 21° at r = 80 M.
  • Ṁ agrees with Font & Ibáñez (1998) to 5 % and the stagnation point to 3.5 M.
  • Together, B1 and B2 reproduce the dependence on Γ: going from Γ = 5/3 to 4/3 changes Ṁ/ṀBHL by a factor 0.87 (Font & Ibáñez: 0.86) and the stagnation distance by 0.60 (0.63), and the cone at r = 20 M narrows from 45° to 31°.

B3: the same wind past a rotating hole (a = 0.9)

B3 repeats B1 with a = 0.9, on a grid from r = 1.0 to 100 M that places the ergosphere on the grid (581 798 steps). It passes: Ė/Ṁ equals the Bernoulli constant to 3 × 10−4.

  • Far from the hole the flow is the same as B1: the cone angles agree for r ≥ 15 M, the densities to 1 % and the stagnation point to 0.2 M.
  • Close to the hole the spin shows: on the downstream axis the pressure is 20 % lower at r = 2 M and 12 % lower at r = 3 M, and the density 16 % lower at r = 2 M; the cone is 0.7–1.4° wider at r = 4–10 M.
  • Ṁ/ṀBHL is 1.3 % below B1, and frame dragging gives the gas a rotation uφ up to 0.11 at r = 2.2 M.

Kerr black hole in a uniform magnetic field (Wald, W1–W4)Passed

A Kerr hole is placed in a magnetic field that is uniform at infinity and aligned with the spin (the vacuum solution of Wald 1974), inside a magnetically dominated plasma as in Komissarov (2005). For a = 0 the field must stay where it is; for a rotating hole the field lines that thread the horizon must rotate and carry the Blandford–Znajek power out of the hole. W1 (a = 0), W2 (a = 0.5) and W3 (a = 0.9) ran on 1024 × 256 cells and W4 (a = 0.99) on 2048 × 256 cells, all to t = 80 M with code release v4r, without a failed inversion, NaN or safety stop, and with relative ∇·B below 10−12.

Magnetised Fishbone–Moncrief torus (FM1)Passed

The magnetised torus is the standard benchmark of GRMHD accretion codes (Gammie, McKinney & Tóth 2003; McKinney & Gammie 2004; the Event Horizon Telescope code comparison, Porth et al. 2019). A Fishbone–Moncrief torus in equilibrium around a Kerr hole (inner edge 6 M, pressure maximum 12 M) holds one weak poloidal field loop with β = 100. The magnetorotational instability (MRI) grows in the torus, the turbulence carries angular momentum outward and the gas accretes. The test exercises everything at once: rotating flow in the Kerr metric, the magnetic field, the floors in the evacuated funnels and the flow through the horizon.

FM1 (a = 0.5, Kerr–Schild, 1536 × 256 cells, r = 1.31–100 M) ran to t = 2000 M in 333 660 steps. Throughout, the relative ∇·B stays at round-off (10−12), with no failed inversion. FM2–FM4 (a = 0.75, 0.9, 0.9375) complete the spin series and are running.

  • Evolution. The torus keeps its shape while the MRI grows; accretion starts at t = 268 M, after 2.8 orbits of the inner edge. The flow is quasi-steady from t ≈ 700 to 1400 M, with a turbulent disc, a thick corona and an evacuated, magnetically dominated funnel threaded by the horizon field.
  • Horizon fluxes. Ė/Ṁ = 0.9339 against 0.933 of McKinney & Gammie (2004), so the efficiency is 0.066 against 0.067. L̇/Ṁ = 2.761 against 2.583 (7 %), and the hole is spun up (s = +1.83 against +1.65).
  • Field and floors. The disc stays weakly magnetised: the normalised horizon flux ϕ ≈ 2–3, far below the magnetically arrested value of about 15. The floors add 0.5 % of the accreted mass, and north and south agree to 3 %.
  • After t ≈ 1000 M the field in the disc decays and Ṁ falls: the expected behaviour of axisymmetric MRI turbulence, which cannot be sustained in two dimensions.

Checks of the scheme

  • Before compilation, every new formula was checked against a line-by-line Python transcription of the scheme. The metric derivatives match finite differences to 2 × 10−10, and the 3+1 split and geometric sources are exact to round-off.
  • Steady geodesic inflow onto a Kerr hole, in both coordinate systems and through the horizon, converges with resolution.
  • Equatorial symmetry, the polar-axis boundary conditions and the corner ∇·B on the axis are preserved to round-off; no mass leaks through the axis.
  • Every run is checked for relative ∇·B < 10−12, no failed inversions, and mass added by the floors below 1 % of the accretion rate.

What a run produces

  • Accretion rates of mass, energy and angular momentum (Ṁ, Ė, L̇) through spheres at four radii, as functions of time
  • Binary VTK snapshots with 50 quantities on the (R, z) half-plane, ready for VisIt and ParaView: densities, velocities, four-velocities, Lorentz factor, Mach numbers, Bernoulli parameter, fluxes, magnetic field, magnetisation, plasma β, the magnetic flux function ψ and more
  • A time series of the magnetic flux on the hole and the MAD parameter φBH
  • Floor statistics, so the effect of numerical floors can be checked
  • Python tools for maps, radial profiles, time series and the Blandford–Znajek analysis

Physics extracted from the output

  • Accretion rate, efficiency and angular-momentum transport
  • Shock structure, sonic surfaces, bound and unbound gas
  • Magnetic flux on the horizon and the magnetically arrested state
  • Blandford–Znajek power and identification of the jet

All quantities are in geometrised units, G = c = M = 1, with lengths and times in M. The manual gives the conversion to physical units.

Working with the code: collaboration

The source code is not publicly distributed. The tests above show that the code works reliably in the (r, θ) plane around Kerr black holes. If you have an astrophysical problem that fits this framework, we are happy to solve it together as a collaboration.

  1. You

    Describe the problem

    The physical system, spin, initial state, magnetic field, how gas is fed, and the quantities you want to measure.
  2. We

    Check feasibility

    We check that the problem is axisymmetric and fits the meridional-plane code, and agree on a plan.
  3. We

    Prepare the set-up

    We write the user header file and the initial and boundary data for your problem.
  4. You

    Run the simulations

    You run the code with the prepared set-up, following the user manual.
  5. Together

    Analyse and publish

    We interpret the results together, and they go into a joint publication.

Contact

To discuss a collaboration, write to us with a short description of your problem.
